preamble: Fourteen solutions are derived from seven common word pairs, each having a single letter interchanged. Clues for these contain the wordplay and letter count for the entry at that number but the definition contained is for the other derived pair member. Fourteen further clues contain single superfluous words, which, when correctly paired, give seven two-word definitions of the original word pairs. The seven remaining clues are normal.

solutions.check: grid and clues read from the Guardian's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Race round right away — where's the fire?

definitions.note: defines HEARTH, this entry's partner from HALE AND HEARTY, as the preamble says

indicators.note: turning something round sends it back the way it came, so the word reads from its end
the abbreviation for right is sent away, so that letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: a relay is a race run by a team in legs
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone told to hurry off asks why the rush, as though there were a fire somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: HALE AND HEARTY swap their H and Y to give YALE and HEARTH; the wordplay builds YALE, but the definition belongs to HEARTH, whose clue at 23 in turn defines YALE.
explanation.definitionFit: The hearth is the floor of a fireplace, so it is exactly where an indoor fire burns.

clue.text: Mistake upsetting two animals

definitions.note: defines SLIP, this entry's partner from SLAP AND TICKLE, as the preamble says

indicators.note: in a down entry, upsetting turns the pair of creatures upside down, so they read from the bottom

parts.note: an elk and a cat, one after the other

explanation.surface: Someone has blundered by unsettling a couple of creatures.
explanation.walkthrough: SLAP AND TICKLE swap their A and I to give SLIP and TACKLE; this wordplay builds TACKLE while the definition belongs to SLIP, and the clue at 6 does the reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: A slip is a small error, the kind of careless mistake made by a slip of the tongue or pen.

clue.text: Make acceptable cycling parody

indicators.note: cycling sends a letter round from one end of the word for parody to the other, like a wheel turning

parts.note: a skit is a short comic parody

explanation.surface: An instruction to tone down a send-up by recycling it into something inoffensive.
explanation.walkthrough: A themed clue: the original pair KISS AND TELL swaps S and T to give KITS and SELL. 'cycling' moves the S of SKIT to the end; 'Make acceptable' defines the partner SELL, not this entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To sell an idea is to persuade people to accept it, which is the partner SELL's meaning here.

clue.text: Joins in middle of week

definitions.note: read as WED'S, Wednesday is, in midweek
definitions.meaning: second meaning, cryptically: Wed (Wednesday) is in the middle of the week

explanation.surface: Someone signs up for something halfway through the working week.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the seven normal clues. The second half is a little sentence, Wed's in middle of week, using the calendar abbreviation for Wednesday.
explanation.definitionFit: To wed two things is to marry or unite them, so weds is a plain synonym of joins.

clue.text: One's moving Table 4, in case

indicators.note: furniture that is moving is being shifted about, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: a means one; the 's is read as is
taken as written
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A restaurant instruction: shift the diner at table four, just in case.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the seven normal clues. Case is grammatical, not a suitcase or a precaution.
explanation.definitionFit: The ablative is a grammatical case of Latin nouns, expressing by, with or from.

clue.text: Set about grabbing large drink? A little one

definitions.note: defines TACKLE, this entry's partner from SLAP AND TICKLE, as the preamble says

indicators.note: something grabbing another thing holds it inside its grip, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a sip is a little drink
L is the abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Someone tucks into a big drink, then is offered only a small one.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds SLIP; the definition at the front is TACKLE's, its partner from SLAP AND TICKLE.
explanation.definitionFit: To tackle a task is to set about it, beginning work on it with determination.

clue.text: Disaffect with surprising set book selection

indicators.note: a surprising arrangement is an unexpected one, so these letters are reshuffled

parts.note: taken as written
a range is a selection of goods on offer

explanation.surface: A set text that surprises its readers and puts them off.
explanation.walkthrough: Book is one of the fourteen superfluous words. Cakes and Ale is a novel by Somerset Maugham.
explanation.definitionFit: To estrange someone is to alienate them, turning their affection away, which is to disaffect them.

clue.text: Make a big thing of sex aid master broke

indicators.note: broke suggests something smashed into pieces, so the letters of these two words are reassembled

parts.note: the run of clue words whose letters, less the superfluous word, are rearranged

explanation.surface: A boss broke a sex aid and is now making a huge fuss about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sex' is one of the puzzle's superfluous words: discount it and 'broke' rearranges the letters of AID MASTER.
explanation.definitionFit: To dramatise a situation is to exaggerate it, treating it as more important or theatrical than it is.

clue.text: Director wanting to know about cleaner system

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for director

indicators.note: about can mean turned about, so the word for inquisitive faces the other way

parts.note: someone nosy always wants to know

explanation.surface: A company director curious about a new cleaning system.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dyson is a brand of vacuum cleaner, named after its inventor James Dyson.

clue.text: Book troubles Phoebe

definitions.note: defines MOON, this entry's partner from MILLS AND BOON, as the preamble says

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for book
ills are troubles or misfortunes

explanation.surface: A novel that brings a woman called Phoebe nothing but trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: MILLS AND BOON swap the M and B to give BILLS and MOON; Phoebe defines MOON, and the clue at 27 defines BILLS.
explanation.definitionFit: Phoebe is one of Saturn's natural satellites, discovered in 1899, so it is a moon.

clue.text: Publishing report jolts Arab leaders

indicators.note: report means something heard, so the word for jolts is taken by its sound; Publishing is the puzzle's superfluous word, attached to it and adding nothing

parts.note: shakes means jolts, as verb or noun

explanation.surface: News coverage of something shocking that has rattled rulers in the Gulf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Publishing' is one of the puzzle's superfluous words, riding on 'Publishing report', where 'report' alone says SHAKES, a word for jolts, is heard rather than spelt.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheikhs are the chiefs of Arab tribes, families or states, so they are leaders in the Arab world.

clue.text: Get lost in South Somerset with nag

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for south
a carper is one who nags and finds fault

explanation.surface: Someone losing their way in the West Country lanes with an old horse.
explanation.walkthrough: Nag looks like a horse but is a complainer. Scarper is British slang for running away; Somerset is a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarper is slang for running off quickly, so it is an order to clear off, like get lost.

clue.text: Games maker's new plan at Olympic opening

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
to intend is to plan

indicators.note: an opening is a beginning, so only the first letter of that word is used

parts.note: its first letter

explanation.surface: A video-game company unveils a scheme at the opening ceremony of the Olympics.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the seven normal clues. Games looks like the Olympic Games, but the games are video games.
explanation.definitionFit: Nintendo is the Japanese company that makes video-game consoles such as the Switch.

clue.text: One very welcome to hold on to post

indicators.note: the words grip the answer inside their run of letters, so only the gripped stretch is kept and the rest let go

parts.note: the letters of these words, where very is a superfluous theme word that interrupts the held run
the outer letters dropped, together with the superfluous word

explanation.surface: Someone who is greeted warmly is invited to keep their job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very' is one of the puzzle's superfluous words: set it aside, and the answer is gripped across the end of 'One' and the start of 'welcome'.
explanation.definitionFit: A newel is the upright post at the foot or turn of a staircase that supports the handrail.

clue.text: First to display chest … ready?

definitions.note: defines RIPE, this entry's partner from PARK AND RIDE, as the preamble says

indicators.note: first means only the leading letter of the following word is taken

parts.note: its first letter
an ark is a chest or coffer, as in the Ark of the Covenant

explanation.surface: Someone about to show off a treasure chest asks whether everyone is ready.
explanation.walkthrough: PARK AND RIDE swap the P and D to give DARK and RIPE; ready defines RIPE here, and the clue at 17 defines DARK.
explanation.definitionFit: Ripe fruit is ready to eat, and a person ripe for something is ready for it.

clue.text: Handle transport working for hotel

parts.note: the hilt is the handle of a sword or dagger
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: A hotel concierge arranging transport that actually works.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hilton is an international chain of hotels founded by Conrad Hilton.

clue.text: Threat regularly produced obedience in school

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the word is kept

parts.note: its first, third and fifth letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: A teacher's constant threats got the class to behave.
explanation.walkthrough: Obedience is superfluous; school is the definition, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To school someone is to teach or drill them, which is what training them means.

clue.text: Rent's close to extortionate — not fair

definitions.note: defines DARK, this entry's partner from PARK AND RIDE, as the preamble says

parts.note: a rip is a rent or tear

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so its final letter is taken

parts.note: its last letter

explanation.surface: A tenant complains that the rent is nearly extortionate and unfair.
explanation.walkthrough: Rent looks like money paid to a landlord but is a tear. The definition is DARK's, from the PARK AND RIDE swap.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair hair or skin is light, so a person who is not fair is dark in colouring.

clue.text: Earlier appeal head disregarded

definitions.note: defines OLDER, this entry's partner from LAW AND ORDER, as the preamble says

indicators.note: a disregarded head is ignored, so the opening letter of the word is left off

parts.note: a draw is an attraction, something with appeal
the head of the word, its first letter

explanation.surface: An appeal lodged earlier, which the head of the court ignored.
explanation.walkthrough: LAW AND ORDER swap the L and R to give RAW and OLDER; earlier defines OLDER, and the clue at 30 defines RAW.
explanation.definitionFit: Something older dates from a prior time, so it is earlier in date.

clue.text: Sky expert back broadcasting — old job in the end protected

indicators.note: something protected is shielded on both sides, so it sits inside the other word

parts.note: the rear is the back

indicators.note: in the end points to the final letter of each of the two words

parts.note: the last letter of each word
a programme that is on is being broadcast

explanation.surface: A Sky TV pundit returns to the airwaves, with an old position kept safe.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the seven normal clues. Sky looks like the satellite broadcaster; the expert is an air ace.
explanation.definitionFit: The Red Baron, Manfred von Richthofen, was the top-scoring fighter ace of the First World War, a master of aerial combat.

clue.text: Shock revelation — money for image promotion suspect

indicators.note: money for image promotion means money stands in place of the promotion letters

parts.note: a shock is a surprise; revelation is the puzzle's superfluous word and adds nothing
PR, public relations, is the business of promoting an image

explanation.surface: A startling disclosure that cash went on spin doctoring makes someone look dodgy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revelation' is one of the puzzle's superfluous words, set aside. 'for' puts M (money) in place of PR (image promotion) in SURPRISE.
explanation.definitionFit: To surmise is to suppose or guess without proof, which is what suspecting something involves.

clue.text: Well! Guide (female) takes Henry inside for a date

parts.note: she is the female pronoun

indicators.note: the king's initial is taken inside another word, so it sits within it

parts.note: per means for a, as in a pound per head
H is the abbreviation for henry, the unit of inductance
D is the abbreviation for date

explanation.surface: A Girl Guide leader takes a boy called Henry along to a dinner date.
explanation.walkthrough: Well is superfluous. Guide (female) suggests a Girl Guide, but the bracketed word gives a pronoun and the definition is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To shepherd people is to steer them carefully along, as a shepherd does a flock, so it means guide.

clue.text: Round city are places for water sports

definitions.note: defines LAKES, this entry's partner from CAKES AND ALE, as the preamble says

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for are, the metric unit of area

indicators.note: brought round, the abbreviation for the City of London faces the other way

parts.note: EC is the postcode for the City of London

explanation.surface: A guide to where to go sailing and swimming around a city.
explanation.walkthrough: CAKES AND ALE swap the C and L to give LAKES and ACE; this definition is for LAKES, and the clue at 24 defines ACE.
explanation.definitionFit: Lakes are large inland bodies of water, used for sailing, rowing and other water sports.

clue.text: Elsie mentioned in song with civil partner — sweet!

indicators.note: in puts the spoken letters inside the word for a two-person song

parts.note: a duet is a song performed with a partner; civil is a superfluous theme word adding nothing

indicators.note: mentioned means spoken, so the name is replaced by letters that sound like it

parts.note: the name Elsie sounds like the letters L and C

explanation.surface: A singer named Elsie appears in a song with her civil partner, and it's lovely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'civil' is one of the puzzle's superfluous words, set aside so that 'song with partner' reads as a two-voice piece. 'mentioned' makes Elsie the spoken letters LC, which go 'in' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dulcet describes a sound that is pleasantly soft and melodious, a sweetness to the ear.

clue.text: Hotel man's drunk alcohol

indicators.note: someone drunk staggers about, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The hotelier has had too much to drink at the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the seven normal clues.
explanation.definitionFit: Methanol is wood alcohol, the simplest alcohol, used as solvent and fuel.

clue.text: End of research centre at top university

definitions.note: defines YALE, this entry's partner from HALE AND HEARTY, as the preamble says

indicators.note: in a down entry, at top means placed above, so the second piece goes first

parts.note: the heart of something is its centre

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: its last letter

explanation.surface: The final stage of a study carried out at a leading university's research centre.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is YALE's, the other half of the HALE AND HEARTY swap.
explanation.definitionFit: Yale is the Ivy League institution of higher learning in New Haven, Connecticut.

clue.text: One visionary poet's not British

definitions.note: defines ACE, this entry's partner from CAKES AND ALE, as the preamble says

indicators.note: not means without, so the British abbreviation is left out of the poet's name

parts.note: William Blake was the visionary poet and painter, with 's
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: A mystical poet who turns out not to be British after all.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition belongs to ACE, from the CAKES AND ALE swap: an ace is the one in a pack of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: The ace is the card with a single pip, counting as one, and on dice a single spot.

clue.text: Play Lincoln or Derby, say?

definitions.meaning: superfluous word; it pairs with sex from 8 across to make sex play, defining SLAP AND TICKLE
surface reading: two English cities, or two famous horse races to bet on
setter's reading: first name of the president Lincoln, and of the ironmaster Darby, whose surname sounds like Derby

explanation.surface: A gambler deciding whether to back a runner in the Lincoln or the Derby.
explanation.walkthrough: Play is superfluous. Abraham Darby pioneered iron smelting with coke at Coalbrookdale, and Derby is said Darby in Britain; the question mark flags the sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the shared forename of President Abraham Lincoln and the industrialist Abraham Darby.

clue.text: Priggish types essentially lacking in culture

indicators.note: essentially points to the essence or core, so only the inner letters are kept and the outer two dropped

parts.note: prudes are priggish, easily shocked people

explanation.surface: Prigs are, at heart, philistines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'essentially' keeps the core of PRUDES, dropping the P and S at its ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Rude in an old sense means rough and unsophisticated, as in rude huts, lacking refinement or learning.

clue.text: They may advertise second leg

definitions.note: defines BILLS, this entry's partner from MILLS AND BOON, as the preamble says

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a second
the leg side in cricket is also called the on side

explanation.surface: Posters promoting the second leg of a cup tie.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is BILLS', from the MILLS AND BOON swap; in cricket the on side and the leg side are the same half of the field.
explanation.definitionFit: Bills are posters stuck up to announce shows or products, as in the sign Stick No Bills.

clue.text: Bird nothing to look at, as we heard earlier

indicators.note: earlier places the second phrase in front of the first
as we heard means by sound, so the spelling may differ

parts.note: to see is to look at
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket

explanation.surface: A dowdy bird that is no beauty, as we were told before.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the seven normal clues. A duck is a batsman's score of zero in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea ducks, such as eiders and scoters, are diving ducks that live on the sea, so a kind of bird.

clue.text: Strips off with women — great!

definitions.note: defines KITS, this entry's partner from KISS AND TELL, as the preamble says

indicators.note: off means taken away, so that letter is removed

parts.note: swell is slang for great
W is the abbreviation for women

explanation.surface: An enthusiastic shout at a strip show with women performing.
explanation.walkthrough: Strips here is the football sense, kits worn by a team; it defines KITS, from the KISS AND TELL swap.
explanation.definitionFit: A team's strip is its kit, the shirts, shorts and socks worn in matches.

clue.text: People suspicious of us — we don't know what they're up for

definitions.text: we don't know what they're up for

indicators.note: suspicious suggests something fishy or not straight, so the letters of these words are rearranged

parts.note: a superfluous theme word: its letters sit in the anagram fodder and are taken back out, giving nothing to the answer
taken as written; the answer also runs backwards through suspicious of us, a coincidence of the surface, not the setter's device

explanation.surface: People eye us warily and can't tell what we are plotting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'People' is one of the puzzle's superfluous words, set aside. 'suspicious' rearranges OF US. The definition plays on 'up': these things are up in the sky, and unidentified.
explanation.definitionFit: Unidentified flying objects are seen overhead with no known origin or purpose, the mystery being their whole point.

clue.text: Green (or red) file fellow's mislaid

definitions.note: defines RAW, this entry's partner from LAW AND ORDER, as the preamble says

indicators.note: something mislaid has gone missing, so that letter is lost from the word

parts.note: a folder is a file for papers
F is the abbreviation for fellow

explanation.surface: An office worker has lost a coloured file, green or perhaps red.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is RAW's, from the LAW AND ORDER swap: raw can mean inexperienced or sore and red.
explanation.definitionFit: A raw recruit is green, untrained; raw skin is red and sore, so both colours fit.

clue.text: They're offered round at private Lisbon dances

parts.note: O is round in shape

indicators.note: dances suggests letters moving about, so the letters of at and Lisbon are rearranged

parts.note: the run of clue words whose letters, less the superfluous word, are rearranged

explanation.surface: Gifts handed around at a private dance party in Portugal's capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'private' is one of the puzzle's superfluous words, set aside; with it gone, 'dances' turns AT LISBON into BLATIONS.
explanation.definitionFit: Oblations are religious offerings, gifts presented to a god, so they are things that get offered.
